Performing initial audit of PKGBUILD to ensure that we can safely run `makepkg`
LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:


<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The `makepkg --printsrcinfo` gate executes only the PKGBUILD's top-level scope. What appears here is standard metadata: variable assignments (`pkgname`, `pkgver`, `pkgrel`, `pkgdesc`, `url`, `license`, `depends`, `makedepends`, `options`, `source`, `sha256sums`) and function definitions (`build`, `check`, `package`). Function bodies are not executed during sourcing, so the `cargo build`, `cargo test`, and `install` commands are out of scope for this gate.

There are no top-level command substitutions ($() or backticks), no `eval`/`base64`/obfuscated constructs, and no commands that fetch or execute code. The `source` array references the project's own upstream GitHub tag (`https://github.com/chaitanyayeleti/kolimi/archive/refs/tags/v0.1.2.tar.gz`), which is expected upstream behavior for a Rust package. A valid 64-character SHA-256 checksum is provided.

`--printsrcinfo` does not download or verify sources at all, so no network request occurs during this gate regardless. Even if the display-escaping (`"`, `<`, etc.) were literal in the file, the worst outcome would be a parse failure, not execution of malicious code.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>
Top-level scope is plain assignments; no code executes during --printsrcinfo.
</summary>
</security_assessment>

<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD follows standard Arch packaging practices for a Rust project. It downloads a versioned source tarball from the project's own GitHub repository with a pinned SHA256 checksum, builds using `cargo --locked` (reproducible builds), runs a targeted test subset, and installs binaries, systemd units, sysusers/tmpfiles configs, and documentation into appropriate `$pkgdir` paths. No suspicious network calls, obfuscation, eval, or off-repo downloads are present. The systemd/service files are sourced from the upstream `packaging/systemd/` directory, which is normal for self-hosted applications. Everything is consistent with legitimate packaging workflow.
</details>
